title: Dandelion: A Spherical Flower for Neural Simulation of Planetary Dynamics
claim: A suite of diverse, natively spherical PDE datasets spanning varied physics and geometries, shown as snapshots, forms a benchmark.
layout: 7 panels in two rows (4 over 3), labeled a–g, spheres
description: A mosaic of seven globe-shaped snapshots, labeled a–g in bold black letters at the top-left of each panel. The top row has four orthographic spheres with red–blue diverging colormaps: (a) wavy jet-stream vorticity bands, (b) fine-scale turbulent vorticity blobs covering the whole sphere, (c) a smooth momentum field with a sharp shock front near the bottom, (d) bold Cahn–Hilliard phase-separation patterns with swirling red and blue domains. The bottom row has three spheres: (e) a cutaway globe with a visible lat–lon mesh showing zonal wind at multiple pressure levels, (f) a cutaway ocean sphere with gray land masses and a rainbow temperature field at depth levels, and (g) a planetary shallow-water azimuthal velocity map. The eye goes first to the vivid saturated panels (b, d), then to the 3D cutaways.
caption: Snapshots of the seven datasets: (a) \galewskytt (vorticity), (b) \mickelintt (vorticity), (c) \shockcapstt (momentum $u$), (d) \cahnhilliardtt ($\phi_0$), (e) \heldsuareztt (zonal wind $u$ at various pressure levels), (f) \oceantt (temperature $T$ at depth levels), and (g) planetswe (azimuthal velocity). (a)--(f) are introduced by this paper; (g) is from The Well [ref].
abstract: Many dynamical processes unfold on the sphere but the default scientific machine learning architectures are Euclidean. Applying these architectures on a regular lat--lon grid causes problems: Cartesian convolutions become distorted at high latitude; 2D FFTs in Fourier neural operators incorrectly assume double periodicity; Cartesian positional encodings in ViTs distort spherical geodesic distances. Recent work moves towards natively spherical primitives, including spherical convolutions (e.g., DeepSphere or DISCO), Spherical Fourier Neural Operators (SFNOs), and geodesic attention. Here we propose Dandelion, a spherical version of Flower---a warp-based neural PDE solver. A Dandelion layer computes a tangent-plane displacement and then transports features along great circles. We obtain a U-Net-like structure by implementing hierarchical pooling entirely in the spherical-harmonic domain. There are thus no convolutions: spatial mixing is achieved only through spherical coordinate changes---or warps. To compare Dandelion with existing spherical architectures, we release an evolving benchmark suite of challenging, natively spherical PDE datasets including a modified Galewsky jet, anomalous chained turbulence, Cahn--Hilliard decomposition, spherical Riemann shocks, Held--Suarez dry atmospheric transport and global ocean dynamics. This new benchmark fills the gap between existing spherical datasets which are either too small and stylized, or much too large (ERA5) for model iteration. Dandelion achieves the best performance on all but one benchmark setting, where the best model is Flower2D, also based on warps. The spherical primitives result in the most physically consistent forecasts.
